By her third month at the university in Nairobi, Vera had started keeping a quiet tally. The campus café hired students for evening shifts, and the manager, a cheerful man from Nyeri, always seemed to have "just filled" the slots, usually with students who had grown up near Nyeri too. Her flatmate Wanjiru had applied twice, with more free hours than anyone. Both times she got a polite no.
In the lab it was similar: the senior student helped the two from his old school first, then looked round for the rest.
One evening Vera said it plainly. "Wanjiru, I don't think it's you. I think it's where people come from."
Wanjiru was quiet, then nodded slowly. "I thought I was imagining it."
Next morning they listed the dates she had applied and asked the student welfare office how café shifts were meant to be given out.

qa.q: How many times had Wanjiru applied for the café shifts?
qa.a: Wanjiru had applied twice.

qa.q: What does Wanjiru mean by 'I thought I was imagining it'?
qa.a: She had sensed something unfair but doubted herself, so hearing Vera name the pattern made her feel less alone and less to blame.

qa.q: What choice did Vera and Wanjiru make the next morning, and why was it a useful turning point?
qa.a: They listed the dates and asked the welfare office how shifts should be given, turning a vague hunch into something that could be checked fairly.

qa.q: How might the café manager see his own hiring if the pattern were pointed out?
qa.a: He may honestly feel he just trusts people he knows, and only seeing the dates side by side might show him that others never got a real chance.

grounding: A student notices café jobs and lab help flowing to people from one home region and names it to the flatmate left out.

In Block C of the girls' hostel, the warden's office opened at eight for room-change requests. Jasleen, second year, sat on the bench outside with her form and noticed something she couldn't unsee. The senior who helped the warden sort requests was from Ludhiana, and so were the three girls who walked out smiling with better rooms. Rajni, from a small town in Jharkhand, had been waiting since October for a room away from the leaking wall. Her form was still "under process".
That night in the mess, Jasleen, who was from Ludhiana herself, admitted it aloud to Rajni. "I got my room in a day. I didn't ask why. I think I know now."
Rajni put down her spoon. "So it wasn't my form."
The next morning Jasleen went back with her and asked the warden to show the waiting list in date order.

qa.a: Rajni wanted a room away from the leaking wall.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she said 'I didn't ask why'?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little guilty, realising her quick room may have come from sharing Ludhiana with the senior, not from fairness. 😔

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen make the next morning, and how could it change things?
qa.a: She went back with Rajni and asked for the waiting list in date order, which makes the date you applied count more than where you come from.

qa.q: How does the long wait look from Rajni's side?
qa.a: For months Rajni probably blamed her own form or bad luck; learning the pattern hurts, but it also frees her from thinking she did something wrong.

grounding: A hostel student sees room changes flow to girls from her own city and names it to the student left waiting.

Dear Anand bhaiya,
Six weeks into the internship, something is bothering me. My manager went to the same college as me, and I get easy trust: "Tarun's from our place, he'll manage." Megha, who sits next to me, came from a smaller college in Nagpur. Her code gets checked line by line. Mine goes through with a glance. Last week the team lunch invite reached everyone from our college first; she heard about it after.
I kept telling myself it was coincidence. Then I counted: of the five people given the new project, four were our alumni. Megha's work is honestly sharper than mine.
I haven't said anything yet. But writing it to you feels like a first step. Next I'd like to ask my manager, gently, how people get picked.
Your brother,
Tarun

qa.q: How many of the five people given the new project were alumni of Tarun's college?
qa.a: Four of the five people given the new project were alumni of Tarun's college.

qa.q: Why had Tarun kept telling himself it was coincidence?
qa.a: Admitting the pattern means admitting he benefits from it, which is uncomfortable, so coincidence felt easier until the count made it hard to ignore.

qa.q: Tarun is deciding whether to speak to the manager. What would make that talk a useful turning point?
qa.a: Asking calmly how people are picked, and pointing to Megha's strong work as an example, could make the manager look at the pattern without feeling accused.

qa.q: What is it like for Megha when her code is checked line by line while Tarun's passes with a glance?
qa.a: Megha may feel she has to prove herself twice over, and hearing about the lunch late could make her feel quietly outside the team.

grounding: An intern notices trust and projects going to people from his own college and names the pattern in a letter.

Swati, you asked why I started that hostel help-desk thing. Okay. I'm Neelam, second year, and it began with me just noticing.
In our hostel, when a senior had spare notes, they went to juniors from their own state. When the canteen needed a student helper, the manager hired "someone from back home." When a first-year from Manipur asked for help with the library portal, three people said they were busy, and ten minutes later helped a boy from their own district.
Nobody was being cruel. It just flowed that way, like water downhill. I did it too. My first instinct was always to help people who spoke my language.
So I started saying it out loud at hostel meetings: "Help keeps going to our own people." People were uncomfortable. But then we set up a shared notes shelf and a sign-up sheet for helpers, open to anyone. Last week the Manipur girl ran it.

qa.q: Who did the canteen manager hire as a student helper?
qa.a: The manager hired "someone from back home."

qa.q: What made Neelam feel the pattern wasn't about cruelty?
qa.a: Neelam noticed it just flowed that way, like water downhill, and even caught the same urge to help people who spoke the same language first.

qa.q: What did Neelam do after noticing the pattern, and why was naming it important?
qa.a: Neelam said it out loud at hostel meetings, which led to a shared notes shelf and an open sign-up sheet, since change began once people could see the pattern.

qa.q: How might the first-year from Manipur have seen the hostel before and after?
qa.a: At first she was turned away while others were helped, which likely felt lonely and unfair; running the shelf later suggests she felt included and trusted.

grounding: A student notices help, jobs and trust flowing towards people from the same region, and naming it becomes the first step towards fairness.

I'm Kiran, and I share a lab bench with Salma in our engineering college in Coimbatore. This semester I watched her do something unusual.
Our department's paid research assistant posts went to six students. Salma pulled up the list on her phone one evening and showed me. All six had gone to the same two schools as the professors. Then she scrolled back: last year, the same.
She didn't sound angry, more puzzled. "The professors probably trust people who remind them of their own school," she said. "Maybe they don't even know they're doing it."
I don't know how nervous she was, but her hands were tight around her phone when she asked the head of department, politely, if the posts could have a written application and a scoring sheet next time.
He frowned, then said he'd think about it. This month's notice board has a form on it. Salma just pointed at it and smiled.

qa.q: How many students got the paid research assistant posts?
qa.a: The posts went to six students.

qa.q: What did Salma seem to think was behind the pattern?
qa.a: She seemed to think the professors trusted students who reminded them of their own schools, perhaps without realising it, which is why she sounded puzzled rather than angry.

qa.q: What did Salma ask the head of department for, and why was it a fair step?
qa.a: She asked for a written application and a scoring sheet, so the posts would be judged on clear criteria rather than on familiarity.

qa.q: How does Kiran see what Salma did?
qa.a: Kiran watched closely and noticed her tight grip on the phone, but is careful not to claim to know how nervous she really was.

grounding: Told by a classmate, it shows a student noticing that opportunities flow to people from the same schools and naming the pattern to make it fairer.

passage: Sachin, you're starting hostel life next month, so let your Kishore mama tell you something I saw at twenty. In our engineering hostel, the mess committee was run by boys from one district, and I was one of them. Every good room, every late-night pass, every second helping of paneer went to our own. I didn't think of it as unfair; it just felt like looking after family. Then one evening a quiet boy from far away, Lalthanga, was refused a room change even though his ceiling leaked onto his books. One of our boys, with a dry room, got a change for a better view. I watched Lalthanga carry his wet books down the stairs, and something turned in me. At the next meeting I said it out loud: "We only help our own." Nobody had ever said it. After that we made the room list by need.

qa.q: Why did Lalthanga need a room change?
qa.a: His ceiling leaked onto his books.

qa.q: What did young Kishore feel watching Lalthanga carry his wet books?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and ashamed, suddenly seeing that looking after his own had been unfair to others.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Saying out loud at the meeting, "We only help our own," which named the pattern and led to a room list by need.

qa.q: How might Lalthanga have felt being refused the room change?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and invisible, carrying wet books while a boy with a dry room got a better view.

grounding: An uncle recalls noticing, as a student, that rooms and favours flowed only to boys from his own district, and naming it.

passage: The relief camp had only forty blankets left, rain was still pouring, and the queue stretched to the road. Kishore, a college volunteer, noticed something odd about the list the camp leader was ticking. Most names came from Rampur, the leader's own village, even though the families from the riverbank colony had arrived first and lost more. "We know Rampur people," the leader said when Vidya, another volunteer, asked. "We trust them." Kishore felt his neck prickle; his own family was from Rampur too. He took a breath. "Sir, we're all helping who we know. Could we give blankets in order of arrival, and check who lost their homes?" The leader stared at him, then at the soaked children from the colony. He tore up the list and started again.

passage: Tanvir had been in the Bengaluru hostel for two years before he noticed it. The mess committee had four paid helper posts for students. All four went to boys from the secretary's home state. The printer room key, the bike parking list, even who got the good corner rooms: it all flowed the same way. Nobody said anything unfair out loud. It just happened. "Nobody plans it. People trust people who sound like them." At the next hostel meeting, Tanvir raised his hand, nervous. "Can we put the helper posts on the notice board, with the rules, before they're filled?" There was an awkward silence. Then the warden said, "Good idea."

Mess committee note, Block C hostel, written by Anand, secretary.
Three part-time helper slots opened this month. All three went to students from our own district. I signed the list myself.
Lalit, a second-year from the north-east wing, had applied first, and his form was complete. When I asked the committee why he was skipped, one member said, "We know our boys, they're reliable." I nodded along at the time.
Once I started looking, I saw it at the counter too: second helpings of dal go faster to people who speak our language.
What I did next: I put Lalit's name back on the list and asked the committee to agree on simple rules (first to apply, full form, rotation every month) and pin them on the notice board.
Saying this out loud at the meeting was awkward. Keeping quiet felt worse.

qa.q: How many helper slots opened this month?
qa.a: Three part-time helper slots opened this month, and all three went to students from the committee's own district.

qa.q: What does Anand's last line suggest about how raising the pattern felt?
qa.a: Anand felt awkward and exposed pointing out a habit the whole committee, Anand included, had shared, but was more uneasy about staying quiet once it was seen.

qa.q: Which step in the note makes the helper jobs fairer, and why?
qa.a: Pinning simple rules such as first to apply, a full form and monthly rotation helps, because a job no longer depends on being from the right district.

qa.q: What is it like for Lalit when the helper slots are filled?
qa.a: Lalit applied first with a complete form and was still skipped, which could leave him feeling excluded and unsure whether effort counts in the hostel.

grounding: Shows a hostel student noticing that jobs and small favours flow toward people from the same district, and naming it with fair rules.
